claim: After the presentation of a visual stimulus, neural processing cascades from low-level sensory areas to increasingly abstract representations in higher-level areas.
source: After the presentation of a visual stimulus, neural processing cascades from low-level sensory areas to increasingly abstract representations in higher-level areas.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in neuroscience supported by extensive prior research.

claim: A reversal in neural processing underlies the generation of mental images as abstract representations are used to construct sensory representations in the absence of sensory input.
source: It is often hypothesised that a reversal in neural processing underlies the generation of mental images as abstract representations are used to construct sensory representations in the absence of sensory input.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the literature, not yet directly demonstrated.

claim: According to predictive processing theories, reversed processing plays a central role in later stages of perception.
source: According to predictive processing theories, such reversed processing also plays a central role in later stages of perception.
evidence: This claim references predictive processing theories from the literature.

claim: Direct experimental evidence of reversals in neural information flow has been missing.
source: Direct experimental evidence of reversals in neural information flow has been missing.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature prior to this study.

claim: During perception, reversals in neural processing alternate with feed-forward processing in an 11 Hz oscillatory pattern.
source: show that, during perception, such reversals alternate with feed-forward processing in an 11 Hz oscillatory pattern.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data and analysis.

claim: There is a reversal of the perceptual feed-forward cascade during imagery.
source: We provide direct evidence for a reversal of the perceptual feed-forward cascade during imagery
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Common feedback processes support both veridical perception and mental imagery.
source: Together, these results show how common feedback processes support both veridical perception and mental imagery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Light waves are transformed into electrical signals that travel via the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus to the visual cortex.
source: Light waves are transformed into electrical signals that travel via the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus to the visual cortex (Card and Moore, 1989; Reid and Alonso, 1995) (but see [Bullier, 2001] for other routes).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Low-level visual features such as orientation and spatial frequency are processed in primary, posterior visual areas.
source: First, low-level visual features such as orientation and spatial frequency are processed in primary, posterior visual areas (Hubel and Wiesel, 1968)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to classic neuroscience research.

claim: Activation spreads forward towards secondary, more anterior visual areas where high-level features such as shape and eventually semantic category are processed.
source: after which activation spreads forward towards secondary, more anterior visual areas where high-level features such as shape and eventually semantic category are processed (Maunsell and Newsome, 1987; Thorpe and Fabre-Thorpe, 2001; Vogels and Orban, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The initial feed-forward flow through the visual hierarchy is completed within 150 ms.
source: This initial feed-forward flow through the visual hierarchy is completed within 150 ms (Seeliger et al., 2018; Thorpe et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: After the initial feed-forward sweep, feedback processes are assumed to further sharpen representations over time until a stable percept is achieved.
source: after which feedback processes are assumed to further sharpen representations over time until a stable percept is achieved (Cauchoix et al., 2014; Kok et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Activation in visual areas can be triggered internally, in the absence of external sensory signals, during mental imagery.
source: Activation in visual areas can also be triggered internally, in the absence of external sensory signals. During mental imagery, information from memory is used to generate rich visual representations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mental imagery.

claim: Neural representations activated during imagery are highly similar to those activated during perception.
source: Neural representations activated during imagery are highly similar to those activated during perception (Dijkstra et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Imagining an object activates similar object representations in high-level visual cortex.
source: Imagining an object activates similar object representations in high-level visual cortex (Dijkstra et al., 2017; Ishai et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2012; Reddy et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Generating a mental image with simple visual features such as oriented gratings or letters is associated with perception-like activation of low-level visual areas.
source: generating a mental image with simple visual features such as oriented gratings or letters is associated with perception-like activation of low-level visual areas (Albers et al., 2013; Pearson et al., 2008; Senden et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The temporal dynamics underlying the activation within the visual system during perception and mental imagery are presumably very different.
source: In contrast, the temporal dynamics underlying the activation within the visual system during perception and mental imagery are presumably very different.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on theoretical considerations.

claim: The neural dynamics of the early stages of perception have been extensively characterised with intracranial electrophysiological recordings in primates.
source: The neural dynamics of the early stages of perception have been extensively characterised with intracranial electrophysiological recordings in primates (Thorpe et al., 1996; Thorpe and Fabre-Thorpe, 2001; Hubel and Wiesel, 1968).
evidence: This is supported by citations to classic neuroscience research.

claim: The neural dynamics of imagery remain unclear.
source: However, the neural dynamics of imagery, i.e. how activation travels through the brain during internally generated visual experience, remain unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Researchers from various fields have proposed that the direction of information flow during internally generated visual experience is reversed compared to perception.
source: Researchers from various fields have proposed that the direction of information flow during internally generated visual experience is reversed compared to perception (Ahissar and Hochstein, 2004; Hochstein and Ahissar, 2002; Kosslyn et al., 2001; Pearson and Keogh, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: During memory recall, high-level, semantic representations were active before low-level, perceptual representations.
source: In line with this idea, a recent study showed that during memory recall, high-level, semantic representations were active before low-level, perceptual representations (Linde-Domingo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: The localization of activation in the Linde-Domingo et al. study was ambiguous such that it is possible that all processing happened within high-level visual cortex.
source: However, the localisation of activation in this study was ambiguous such that it is possible that all processing happened within high-level visual cortex but that only the dimension to which the neurons were sensitive changed from abstract features to perceptual features over time
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of a cited study based on inference.

claim: Memory recall was not directly compared with memory encoding in the Linde-Domingo et al. study.
source: Moreover, memory recall was not directly compared with memory encoding.
evidence: This is a statement about the design of a cited study.

claim: According to predictive processing theories, the brain deals with the inherent ambiguity of incoming sensory signals by incorporating prior knowledge about the world.
source: According to predictive processing (PP) theories, reversals of information flow also play an important role during perception. PP states that the brain deals with the inherent ambiguity of incoming sensory signals by incorporating prior knowledge about the world (Helmholtz, 1925).
evidence: This is a description of predictive processing theory supported by a citation.

claim: Prior knowledge is used to generate top-down sensory predictions which are compared to the bottom-up sensory input.
source: This knowledge is used to generate top-down sensory predictions which are compared to the bottom-up sensory input.
evidence: This is a description of predictive processing theory.

claim: Perceptual inference is accomplished by iteratively updating the model of the world until the difference between prediction and input is minimised.
source: Perceptual inference is then accomplished by iteratively updating the model of the world until the difference between prediction and input is minimised (Friston, 2005; Knill and Pouget, 2004).
evidence: This is a description of predictive processing theory supported by citations.

claim: The neural dynamics of stimulus information during perception should be characterised by an interplay between feed-forward and feedback sweeps.
source: Therefore, the neural dynamics of stimulus information during perception should be characterised by an interplay between feed-forward and feedback sweeps.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from predictive processing theory.

claim: Simulations based on PP models predict that recurrent dynamics are dominated by slow-wave oscillations.
source: Simulations based on PP models predict that these recurrent dynamics are dominated by slow-wave oscillations (Bastos et al., 2012; Lozano-Soldevilla and VanRullen, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: Twenty-five participants executed a retro-cue task while MEG was measured.
source: Twenty-five participants executed a retro-cue task while MEG was measured.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: During the task, two consecutive stimuli were presented, a face and a house or a house and a face, followed by a cue indicating whether participants had to imagine the first or the second stimulus.
source: During the task, two consecutive stimuli were presented, a face and a house or a house and a face, followed by a cue indicating whether participants had to imagine the first or the second stimulus.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: There were eight exemplars per stimulus category which were chosen to be highly similar to minimise variation in low-level details within categories and to maximise between-category differences.
source: There were eight exemplars per stimulus category which were chosen to be highly similar to minimise variation in low-level details within categories and to maximise between-category differences.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: An accuracy of 89.9% (SD = 5.4%) on catch trials indicated that participants did indeed imagine the stimuli with a high degree of visual detail.
source: An accuracy of 89.9% (SD = 5.4%) indicated that participants did indeed imagine the stimuli with a high degree of visual detail.
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the study.

claim: Perceptual content could be decoded significantly better than chance level at 70 ms after stimulus onset.
source: Perceptual content could be decoded significantly better than chance level at 70 ms after stimulus onset (Dijkstra et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data and a citation.

claim: Visual information is detectable in early visual cortex from 50 ms onwards according to intracranial and MEG studies.
source: This is in line with intracranial and MEG studies which showed that visual information is detectable in early visual cortex from 50 ms onwards (Thorpe and Fabre-Thorpe, 2001; Ramkumar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Around 130 ms, high-level object representations first get activated according to intracranial and scalp electrophysiology.

evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Source reconstruction of the sensor-level activation patterns at different time points shows that stimulus information spreads from low-level visual areas towards higher-level visual areas during the 70-130 ms period.
source: In line with this, source reconstruction of the sensor-level activation patterns at different time points shows that stimulus information (i.e. the difference in activation between faces and houses [Haufe et al., 2014] spreads from low-level visual areas towards higher-level visual areas during this period (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Cross-correlation between the information flow in early visual cortex (EVC) and inferior temporal cortex (IT) confirms that stimulus information is available in low-level EVC 26.3 ms (CI = 13.1 to 32.9 ms) before it reaches high-level IT.
source: Furthermore, cross-correlation between the information flow in early visual cortex (EVC) and inferior temporal cortex (IT; Figure 1B) confirms that stimulus information is available in low-level EVC 26.3 ms (CI = 13.1 to 32.9 ms) before it reaches high-level IT.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The distance to the hyperplane indicates the amount of classifier evidence present in the data.
source: The distance to the hyperplane indicates the amount of classifier evidence present in the data.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the interpretation of classifier outputs.

claim: Distance measures have previously been used as a measure of model activation.
source: Distance measures have previously been used as a measure of model activation (Kerrén et al., 2018; Linde-Domingo et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior methodological work.

claim: Distance measures have been linked to reaction time measurements.
source: and have been linked to reaction time measurements (Grootswagers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There is a significant main effect of perception time on imagery reactivation time (t(98160) = −5.403, p=6.58e-8) with a negative slope (β0 = 2.05, SD = 0.28; β1 = −1.17,SD = 0.22).
source: The model showed a significant main effect of perception time (t(98160) = −5.403, p=6.58e-8) with a negative slope (β0 = 2.05, SD = 0.28; β1 = −1.17,SD = 0.22)

claim: Cross-correlation between realigned signals shows that information in IT precedes information in EVC by 11.2 ms (CI = 0 to 29.9 ms).
source: Cross-correlation between these realigned signals shows that information in IT precedes information in EVC by 11.2 ms (CI = 0 to 29.9 ms).

claim: Before realignment, time-locked decoding during imagery only revealed a small amount of information in high-level visual cortex.

source: The sequential reactivation disappeared when using shuffled classifiers as perception time did not significantly predict imagery reactivation time anymore (t(98160) = −0.762, p=0.446).

source: Interestingly, during the first 400 ms of perception, there seems to be an oscillatory pattern in the relationship between perception time and imagery reactivation time, where positive and negative slopes alternate.

source: This pattern repeats four times in 400 ms, roughly reflecting an alpha oscillation.

source: There was a significant increase in 10 Hz power between 80 and 315 ms after stimulus onset during perception (all FDR corrected p-values below 0.003).

source: Furthermore, a Fast Fourier Transform over the first 400 ms revealed that the difference in power was limited to the 11.2 Hz frequency (Figure 4B right, p=0.001).

claim: During perception, stimulus information travels up and down the visual hierarchy aligned to the alpha frequency.
source: These results indicate that, during perception, stimulus information travels up and down the visual hierarchy aligned to the alpha frequency.

source: The average decreasing (feed-forward) slope was −0.69 (CI = −2.05 to −0.35)

source: As expected, the diagonal, reflecting training and testing on the same phase, was always positive.

claim: Training and testing on different phases tended to be associated with negative slopes.
source: In contrast, training and testing on different phases tended to be associated with negative slopes.

claim: The Recurrence Index (RI) was significantly larger than zero for the true data (RI = 1.83, CI = 1.71 to 1.94, p < 0.0001).
source: The RI was significantly larger than zero for the true data (RI = 1.83, CI = 1.71 to 1.94, p < 0.0001)

claim: During perception, stimulus information flows up and down the visual hierarchy in feedback and feed-forward phases.
source: This confirms that during perception, stimulus information flows up and down the visual hierarchy in feedback and feed-forward phases.

source: confirming that the perceptual recurrence is most strongly aligned to the alpha frequency.

source: The results show that the recurrence pattern is indeed restricted the first 400 ms after stimulus onset.

source: Neighbouring phases indeed show a significantly higher RI (M = 0.073, CI = 0.069 to 0.076) than other phases (M = 0.002, CI = −0.0004 to 0.005, p < 0.0001)

claim: Recurrence was restricted to a small number of cycles.
source: confirming that recurrence was restricted to a small number of cycles.

claim: Early perception processes are reactivated in reverse order during imagery.
source: First, we showed that early perception processes are reactivated in reverse order during imagery
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the data.

claim: During imagery, activation flows from high-level visual areas down to low-level areas over time.
source: demonstrating that during imagery, activation flows from high-level visual areas down to low-level areas over time.

claim: For later stages of perception, there is an oscillatory pattern of alternating positive and negative relations with imagery reactivation, indicating recurrent stimulus processing up and down the visual hierarchy aligned to an 11 Hz oscillation.
source: Second, for later stages of perception, we found an oscillatory pattern of alternating positive and negative relations with imagery reactivation, indicating recurrent stimulus processing up and down the visual hierarchy aligned to an 11 Hz oscillation.

claim: Recurrence during perception was restricted to neighbouring phases, suggesting that the format of neural stimulus representations changed with subsequent cycles of recurrent processing.
source: Finally, by focusing on the identified feed-forward and feedback phases, we showed that recurrence during perception was restricted to neighbouring phases, suggesting that the format of neural stimulus representations changed with subsequent cycles of recurrent processing.
evidence: This is a conclusion of the study based on the data.

claim: During imagery, stimulus representations are activated via feedback processing.
source: Together, these findings indicate that during imagery, stimulus representations are activated via feedback processing
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: During perception, stimulus representations are iteratively updated through cycles of recurrent processing.
source: whereas during perception, stimulus representations are iteratively updated through cycles of recurrent processing.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: The results are in line with predictive processing (PP) theories.
source: Our results are neatly in line with predictive processing (PP) theories.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of existing theory.

claim: According to PP, recurrent processing during perception reflects dynamic hypothesis testing.
source: According to PP, recurrent processing during perception reflects dynamic hypothesis testing (Bastos et al., 2012; Friston, 2005; Kersten et al., 2004; Knill and Pouget, 2004).
evidence: This is a description of PP theory supported by citations.

claim: Perceptual inference is assumed to be accomplished via an interplay between top-down prediction signals encoding perceptual hypotheses and bottom-up prediction errors encoding the sensory signal unexplained by these hypotheses.
source: Specifically, perceptual inference is assumed to be accomplished via an interplay between top-down prediction signals encoding perceptual hypotheses and bottom-up prediction errors encoding the sensory signal unexplained by these hypotheses.
evidence: This is a description of PP theory.

claim: Inferring the cause of sensory input is done by iteratively updating the perceptual hypothesis until the prediction error is minimised.
source: Inferring the cause of sensory input is done by iteratively updating the perceptual hypothesis until the prediction error is minimised, in line with the dynamically changing representations observed here.
evidence: This is a description of PP theory and how it relates to the findings.

claim: Recurrent processing is assumed to happen hierarchically such that each level is activated by both bottom-up evidence as well as top-down predictions.
source: Importantly, recurrent processing is assumed to happen hierarchically such that each level is activated by both bottom-up evidence as well as top-down predictions (Friston, 2005).
evidence: This is a description of PP theory supported by a citation.

claim: The observation that feed-forward and feedback sweeps proceeded at the same speed is in line with hierarchical recurrent processing in PP.
source: This is in line with our observation that feed-forward and feedback sweeps proceeded at the same speed.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the findings to PP theory.

claim: The current study is the first to show perceptual updating cycles empirically in humans.
source: To our knowledge, the current study is the first to show these perceptual updating cycles empirically in humans.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: In the current task context, the perceptual inference process was completed in approximately four updating cycles.
source: Furthermore, our results suggest that in the current task context, the perceptual inference process was completed in approximately four updating cycles.

claim: All perceptual feed-forward sweeps showed a negative relationship with the same imagery time window.

source: and all perceptual feedback sweeps showed a negative relationship with that same imagery time window.

claim: The imagery feedback flow contained the complete stimulus representation that was inferred via recurrent cycles during perception.
source: This suggests that the imagery feedback flow contained the complete stimulus representation that was inferred via recurrent cycles during perception.

claim: Imagery uses the same predictive processes that underlie perceptual inference to run off-line simulations of sensory representations under different hypotheses.
source: This result fits with the idea that imagery uses the same predictive processes that underlie perceptual inference to run off-line simulations of sensory representations under different hypotheses (Dijkstra et al., 2019; Gershman, 2019; Grush, 2004; Hobson and Friston, 2012; Moulton and Kosslyn, 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of existing theory, supported by citations.

claim: During imagery, there is no bottom-up sensory input prompting hypothesis updating.
source: In contrast to perception, during imagery, there is no bottom-up sensory input prompting hypothesis updating.
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction between perception and imagery.

claim: During imagery, the perceptual cause is given and feedback connections are used to generate the corresponding low-level sensory representation based on the mapping that was learned during perception.
source: Instead, the perceptual cause is given and feedback connections are used to generate the corresponding low-level sensory representation based on the mapping that was learned during perception.
evidence: This is an interpretation of how imagery works based on the findings.

claim: The initial feedforward sweep during perception does not seem to be influenced by attention.
source: However, a recent study showed that the initial feedforward sweep during perception does not seem to be influenced by attention (Alilović et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Modelling work using Convolutional Neural Networks (CCNs) has shown that the MEG signal during perception reflects activation of hierarchically increasing complex features over time.
source: Moreover, modelling work using Convolutional Neural Networks (CCNs) has shown that the MEG signal during perception does reflect activation of hierarchically increasing complex features over time (Seeliger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to modeling work.

claim: While similar neural representations are activated during imagery and perception, the neural dynamics underlying this activation are different.
source: we show that, while similar neural representations are activated during imagery and perception, the neural dynamics underlying this activation are different.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: Perception is characterised by recurrent processing.
source: Whereas perception is characterised by recurrent processing

claim: Imagery is dominated by top-down feedback processing.
source: imagery is dominated by top-down feedback processing.

claim: During perception, high-level causes of sensory input are inferred.
source: These results are in line with the idea that during perception, high-level causes of sensory input are inferred

claim: During imagery, the inferred mapping is reversed to generate sensory representations given these causes.

claim: There is a fundamental asymmetry in information processing between perception and imagery.
source: This highlights a fundamental asymmetry in information processing between perception and imagery

claim: Thirty human volunteers with normal or corrected-to-normal vision gave written informed consent and participated in the study.
source: We assumed a medium effect size (d = 0.6) which, to reach a power of 0.8, required twenty four participants. To take into account drop-out, thirty human volunteers with normal or corrected-to-normal vision gave written informed consent and participated in the study.
evidence: This describes the participant recruitment for the study.

claim: Five participants were excluded from the analysis.
source: Five participants were excluded: two because of movement in the scanner (movement exceeded 15 mm), two due to incorrect execution of the task (less than 50% correct on the catch trials, as described below) and one due to technical problems.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria applied in the study.

claim: Twenty-five participants (mean age 28.6, SD = 7.62) remained for the final analysis.
source: Twenty-five participants (mean age 28.6, SD = 7.62) remained for the final analysis.
evidence: This describes the final sample for the study.

claim: The study was approved by the local ethics committee and conducted according to the corresponding ethical guidelines (CMO Arnhem-Nijmegen).
source: The study was approved by the local ethics committee and conducted according to the corresponding ethical guidelines (CMO Arnhem-Nijmegen).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Data were recorded at 1200 Hz using a 275-channel MEG system with axial gradiometers.
source: Data were recorded at 1200 Hz using a 275-channel MEG system with axial gradiometers (VSM/CTF Systems, Coquitlam, BC, Canada).
evidence: This describes the data acquisition method.

source: For technical reasons, data from five sensors (MRF66, MLC11, MLC32, MLF62, MLO33) were not recorded.

claim: Head movement was kept below 8 mm in most participants.
source: This way, head movement was kept below 8 mm in most participants.

source: After artefact rejection, on average 108 perception face trials, 107 perception house trials, 105 imagery face trials and 106 imagery house trials remained for analysis.
evidence: This describes the number of trials included in the analysis.

claim: A linear discriminant analysis (LDA) classifier with a shrinkage regularisation parameter of 0.05 was used to decode the stimulus category per perception time point.
source: Specifically, to decode the stimulus category per perception time point, we used a linear discriminant analysis (LDA) classifier with the activity from the 270 MEG sensors as features and a shrinkage regularisation parameter of 0.05 (see [Mostert et al., 2016] for more details).
evidence: This describes the machine learning method used in the study.

claim: A five-fold cross-validation procedure was implemented to prevent auto-correlations in the signal from inflating decoding accuracy.
source: To circumvent this, a five-fold cross-validation procedure was implemented where for each fold the classifier was trained on 80% of the trials and tested on the other 20%.
evidence: This describes the cross-validation method used to ensure valid results.

claim: The data were demeaned by subtracting the mean over trials per time point and per sensor to force the classifier to leverage relative changes in the multivariate signal.
source: Because the amplitude of the signal is usually smaller during imagery than during perception (Kosslyn et al., 2001; Pearson and Keogh, 2019), we demeaned the data by subtracting the mean over trials per time point and per sensor. This forced the classifier to leverage relative changes in the multivariate signal while avoiding the confounding effect of having global changes in amplitude.
evidence: This describes a preprocessing step to control for amplitude differences.
